template.name: Opening: Lucy in Florence – The Question of Authenticity

assignments.text:
Lucy waited for nearly ten minutes. Then she began to get tired. The beggars
worried her, the dust blew in her eyes, and she remembered that a young girl
ought not to loiter in public places. She descended slowly into the Piazza with
the intention of rejoining Miss Lavish, who was really almost too original. But
at that moment Miss Lavish and her local-colour box moved also, and disappeared
down a side street, both gesticulating largely. Tears of indignation came to
Lucy’s eyes partly because Miss Lavish had jilted her, partly because she had
taken her Baedeker. How could she find her way home? How could she find her way
about in Santa Croce? Her first morning was ruined, and she might never be in
Florence again. A few minutes ago she had been all high spirits, talking as a
woman of culture, and half persuading herself that she was full of originality.
Now she entered the church depressed and humiliated, not even able to remember
whether it was built by the Franciscans or the Dominicans. Of course, it must
be a wonderful building. But how like a barn! And how very cold! Of course, it
contained frescoes by Giotto, in the presence of whose tactile values she was
capable of feeling what was proper. But who was to tell her which they were?
She walked about disdainfully, unwilling to be enthusiastic over monuments of
uncertain authorship or date. There was no one even to tell her which, of all
the sepulchral slabs that paved the nave and transepts, was the one that was
really beautiful, the one that had been most praised by Mr. Ruskin.
assignments.summary: Lucy waits for Miss Lavish, grows tired and anxious, realizes she has been abandoned and her Baedeker taken, and enters Santa Croce feeling humiliated, unable to remember basic facts and fearful of appearing ignorant.
assignments.best_quote: A few minutes ago she had been all high spirits, talking as a woman of culture, and half persuading herself that she was full of originality. Now she entered the church depressed and humiliated, not even able to remember whether it was built by the Franciscans or the Dominicans.

assignments.text:
She did not answer. From her feet the ground sloped sharply into view, and
violets ran down in rivulets and streams and cataracts, irrigating the hillside
with blue, eddying round the tree stems collecting into pools in the hollows,
covering the grass with spots of azure foam. But never again were they in such
profusion; this terrace was the well-head, the primal source whence beauty
gushed out to water the earth.
assignments.summary: Lucy observes violets flowing down the hillside in water-like formations, recognizing the terrace as the primal wellspring of all beauty flowing into the world.
assignments.best_quote: From her feet the ground sloped sharply into view, and violets ran down in rivulets and streams and cataracts, irrigating the hillside with blue, eddying round the tree stems collecting into pools in the hollows, covering the grass with spots of azure foam. But never again were they in such profusion; this terrace was the well-head, the primal source whence beauty gushed out to water the earth.

assignments.text:
“No, I have said nothing indiscreet. I foresaw at Florence that her quiet,
uneventful childhood must end, and it has ended. I realized dimly enough that
she might take some momentous step. She has taken it. She has learnt—you
will let me talk freely, as I have begun freely—she has learnt what it is
to love: the greatest lesson, some people will tell you, that our earthly life
provides.” It was now time for him to wave his hat at the approaching trio. He
did not omit to do so. “She has learnt through you,” and if his voice was still
clerical, it was now also sincere; “let it be your care that her knowledge is
profitable to her.”
assignments.summary: Mr. Beebe, assuming his clerical role, blesses the engagement and speaks of Lucy having learned to love—the greatest life lesson—and calls Cecil to ensure her knowledge is profitable.
assignments.best_quote: she has learnt what it is to love: the greatest lesson, some people will tell you, that our earthly life provides

template.name: The Pension Bertolini: Class, Courtesy, and the Comedy of Manners
preferred_arcs: The Pension Bertolini as theatre of class

assignments.arc_name: The Pension Bertolini as theatre of class
assignments.text:
“No!” exclaimed Mr. Emerson, in much too loud a voice for church. “Remember
nothing of the sort! Built by faith indeed! That simply means the workmen
weren’t paid properly. And as for the frescoes, I see no truth in them. Look at
that fat man in blue! He must weigh as much as I do, and he is shooting into
the sky like an air balloon.”
assignments.summary: Mr. Emerson loudly interrupts the lecturer, ridiculing the notion of medieval faith (arguing workers were unpaid) and criticizing the anatomical implausibility of the Giotto fresco.
assignments.best_quote: Built by faith indeed! That simply means the workmen weren't paid properly. And as for the frescoes, I see no truth in them. Look at that fat man in blue! He must weigh as much as I do, and he is shooting into the sky like an air balloon.

assignments.arc_name: The Pension Bertolini as theatre of class
assignments.text:
He was referring to the fresco of the “Ascension of St. John.” Inside, the
lecturer’s voice faltered, as well it might. The audience shifted uneasily, and
so did Lucy. She was sure that she ought not to be with these men; but they had
cast a spell over her. They were so serious and so strange that she could not
remember how to behave.
assignments.summary: Lucy feels uncomfortable being associated with the Emersons' outburst; she senses they have cast a spell over her, but she cannot reconcile this with proper behaviour.

assignments.arc_name: The Pension Bertolini as theatre of class
assignments.text:
But Mr. Emerson, contrite and unhappy, hurried away to apologize to the Rev.
Cuthbert Eager. Lucy, apparently absorbed in a lunette, could hear the lecture
again interrupted, the anxious, aggressive voice of the old man, the curt,
injured replies of his opponent. The son, who took every little contretemps as
if it were a tragedy, was listening also.
assignments.summary: Lucy listens to the muffled conflict between Mr. Emerson and Mr. Eager while George, sensitive to social tension, listens as well.

assignments.text:
They began to sort their clothes for packing, for there was no time to lose, if
they were to catch the train to Rome. Lucy, when admonished, began to move to
and fro between the rooms, more conscious of the discomforts of packing by
candlelight than of a subtler ill. Charlotte, who was practical without
ability, knelt by the side of an empty trunk, vainly endeavouring to pave it
with books of varying thickness and size. She gave two or three sighs, for the
stooping posture hurt her back, and, for all her diplomacy, she felt that she
was growing old. The girl heard her as she entered the room, and was seized
with one of those emotional impulses to which she could never attribute a
cause. She only felt that the candle would burn better, the packing go easier,
the world be happier, if she could give and receive some human love. The
impulse had come before to-day, but never so strongly. She knelt down by her
cousin’s side and took her in her arms.
assignments.summary: As they pack by candlelight, Charlotte struggles with an empty trunk while sighing from back pain. Lucy is seized with an impulse to comfort her and embraces her, seeking human connection.
assignments.best_quote: She only felt that the candle would burn better, the packing go easier, the world be happier, if she could give and receive some human love.

assignments.arc_name: The Pension Bertolini as theatre of class
assignments.text:
But Lucy remembered the vendor of photographs and said, “No, don’t be rude to
him.” Then with a catching of her breath, she murmured: “Mr. Eager and
Charlotte, dreadful frozen Charlotte. How cruel she would be to a man like
that!”
assignments.summary: Lucy tells George not to be rude to the cabman and reflects on how cruelly Charlotte would treat such a person.
assignments.best_quote: No, don't be rude to him. How cruel she would be to a man like that!

template.name: Narrative Mirrors: How Forster Shows What Lucy Cannot See

assignments.text:
So did Cecil; but Italy had quickened Cecil, not to tolerance, but to
irritation. He saw that the local society was narrow, but, instead of saying,
“Does that very much matter?” he rebelled, and tried to substitute for it the
society he called broad. He did not realize that Lucy had consecrated her
environment by the thousand little civilities that create a tenderness in time,
and that though her eyes saw its defects, her heart refused to despise it
entirely. Nor did he realize a more important point—that if she was too
great for this society, she was too great for all society, and had reached the
stage where personal intercourse would alone satisfy her. A rebel she was, but
not of the kind he understood—a rebel who desired, not a wider
dwelling-room, but equality beside the man she loved. For Italy was offering
her the most priceless of all possessions—her own soul.
assignments.summary: While Italy irritated Cecil into rebellion against narrow society, it gave Lucy self-knowledge; Cecil fails to understand that she seeks not wider society but equality with the man she loves.
assignments.best_quote: Italy was offering her the most priceless of all possessions—her own soul.

assignments.text:
“The Emersons who were at Florence, do you mean? No, I don’t suppose it will
prove to be them. It is probably a long cry from them to friends of Mr. Vyse’s.
Oh, Mrs. Honeychurch, the oddest people! The queerest people! For our part we
liked them, didn’t we?” He appealed to Lucy. “There was a great scene over some
violets. They picked violets and filled all the vases in the room of these very
Miss Alans who have failed to come to Cissie Villa. Poor little ladies! So
shocked and so pleased. It used to be one of Miss Catharine’s great stories.
‘My dear sister loves flowers,’ it began. They found the whole room a mass of
blue—vases and jugs—and the story ends with ‘So ungentlemanly and
yet so beautiful.’ It is all very difficult. Yes, I always connect those
Florentine Emersons with violets.”
assignments.summary: Mr Beebe recounts the story of the Emerson men filling the Miss Alans' room with violets—a tale that illustrates their lack of propriety and genuine beauty of spirit.
assignments.best_quote: So ungentlemanly and yet so beautiful.

assignments.text:
“Hullo!” he called, and leant out of the smoking-room window. He seemed in high
spirits. “I was hoping you’d come. I heard you all bear-gardening, but there’s
better fun up here. I, even I, have won a great victory for the Comic Muse.
George Meredith’s right—the cause of Comedy and the cause of Truth are
really the same; and I, even I, have found tenants for the distressful Cissie
Villa. Don’t be angry! Don’t be angry! You’ll forgive me when you hear it all.”
assignments.summary: Cecil emerges triumphantly from the smoking-room, claiming victory in finding tenants for Cissie Villa and invoking Meredith about comedy and truth.
assignments.best_quote: George Meredith's right—the cause of Comedy and the cause of Truth are really the same; and I, even I, have found tenants for the distressful Cissie Villa.

assignments.text:
“I taught him,” he quavered, “to trust in love. I said: ‘When love comes, that
is reality.’ I said: ‘Passion does not blind. No. Passion is sanity, and the
woman you love, she is the only person you will ever really understand.’” He
sighed: “True, everlastingly true, though my day is over, and though there is
the result. Poor boy! He is so sorry! He said he knew it was madness when you
brought your cousin in; that whatever you felt you did not mean. Yet”—his
voice gathered strength: he spoke out to make certain—“Miss Honeychurch,
do you remember Italy?”
assignments.summary: Mr. Emerson confesses he taught George to trust in love and passion, expressing his philosophy that genuine love is the deepest sanity and understanding; he ends by asking if Lucy remembers Italy.
assignments.best_quote: When love comes, that is reality. Passion does not blind. No. Passion is sanity, and the woman you love, she is the only person you will ever really understand

template.name: George Emerson's Philosophy: Being Yourself in an Unforgiving World
preferred_arcs: George Emerson's philosophy of being yourself

assignments.text:
“Oh, dear!” breathed the little old lady, and shuddered as if all the winds of
heaven had entered the apartment. “Gentlemen sometimes do not realize—”
Her voice faded away, but Miss Bartlett seemed to understand and a conversation
developed, in which gentlemen who did not thoroughly realize played a principal
part. Lucy, not realizing either, was reduced to literature. Taking up
Baedeker’s Handbook to Northern Italy, she committed to memory the most
important dates of Florentine History. For she was determined to enjoy herself
on the morrow. Thus the half-hour crept profitably away, and at last Miss
Bartlett rose with a sigh, and said:
assignments.summary: The old lady shudders and begins a discourse with Charlotte about male ignorance; Lucy, unable to participate in the abstract conversation, distracts herself by studying Baedeker's guide.
assignments.best_quote: Lucy, not realizing either, was reduced to literature. Taking up Baedeker's Handbook to Northern Italy, she committed to memory the most important dates of Florentine History.

assignments.text:
“I think I shall go out,” said Lucy. “I want to go round the town in the
circular tram—on the platform by the driver.”
assignments.summary: Lucy declares that she will go out alone on the circular tram, riding on the platform beside the driver.

assignments.text:
She could not carry her request any further. The river was rushing below them,
almost black in the advancing night. He had thrown her photographs into it, and
then he had told her the reason. It struck her that it was hopeless to look for
chivalry in such a man. He would do her no harm by idle gossip; he was
trustworthy, intelligent, and even kind; he might even have a high opinion of
her. But he lacked chivalry; his thoughts, like his behaviour, would not be
modified by awe. It was useless to say to him, “And would you—” and hope
that he would complete the sentence for himself, averting his eyes from her
nakedness like the knight in that beautiful picture. She had been in his arms,
and he remembered it, just as he remembered the blood on the photographs that
she had bought in Alinari’s shop. It was not exactly that a man had died;
something had happened to the living: they had come to a situation where
character tells, and where childhood enters upon the branching paths of Youth.
assignments.summary: Lucy reflects that George lacks chivalry; he is trustworthy and kind but not bound by awe or deference. She realizes that a profound shift has occurred: they have entered a moment where character and authenticity matter more than propriety.
assignments.best_quote: they had come to a situation where character tells, and where childhood enters upon the branching paths of Youth.

assignments.arc_name: George Emerson's philosophy of being yourself
assignments.text:
George had turned at the sound of her arrival. For a moment he contemplated
her, as one who had fallen out of heaven. He saw radiant joy in her face, he
saw the flowers beat against her dress in blue waves. The bushes above them
closed. He stepped quickly forward and kissed her.
assignments.summary: George, moved by Lucy's radiant joy and the beauty of the violets around her, steps forward and kisses her impulsively.
assignments.best_quote: He saw radiant joy in her face, he saw the flowers beat against her dress in blue waves. The bushes above them closed. He stepped quickly forward and kissed her.

assignments.text: “No—” she gasped, and, for the second time, was kissed by him.
assignments.summary: George kisses Lucy in the shrubbery, and she gasps in protest but does not resist.
assignments.best_quote: "No—" she gasped, and, for the second time, was kissed by him.

assignments.text: “I propose to speak to him,” said she.
assignments.summary: Lucy declares her intention to speak to George directly and resolve the matter herself.

assignments.text:
Miss Bartlett returned the embrace with tenderness and warmth. But she was not
a stupid woman, and she knew perfectly well that Lucy did not love her, but
needed her to love. For it was in ominous tones that she said, after a long
pause:
assignments.summary: Charlotte returns Lucy's embrace with warmth but understands the emotional transaction: Lucy needs her love, not the reverse. After a pause, Charlotte speaks in ominous tones.
assignments.best_quote: she knew perfectly well that Lucy did not love her, but needed her to love

assignments.text:
“I could as easily tell you what tune she’ll play next. There was simply the
sense that she had found wings, and meant to use them. I can show you a
beautiful picture in my Italian diary: Miss Honeychurch as a kite, Miss
Bartlett holding the string. Picture number two: the string breaks.”
assignments.summary: Mr. Beebe describes an image from his Italian diary: Lucy as a kite with Charlotte holding the string, and the string breaking—symbolizing liberation.
assignments.best_quote: Miss Honeychurch as a kite, Miss Bartlett holding the string. Picture number two: the string breaks

assignments.text:
He had known Lucy for several years, but only as a commonplace girl who
happened to be musical. He could still remember his depression that afternoon
at Rome, when she and her terrible cousin fell on him out of the blue, and
demanded to be taken to St. Peter’s. That day she had seemed a typical
tourist—shrill, crude, and gaunt with travel. But Italy worked some
marvel in her. It gave her light, and—which he held more
precious—it gave her shadow. Soon he detected in her a wonderful
reticence. She was like a woman of Leonardo da Vinci’s, whom we love not so
much for herself as for the things that she will not tell us. The things are
assuredly not of this life; no woman of Leonardo’s could have anything so
vulgar as a “story.” She did develop most wonderfully day by day.
assignments.summary: Cecil recalls how Italy transformed Lucy from a crude tourist into someone mysterious and ethereal, like a Leonardo da Vinci painting—reticent and shadowed rather than bright.
assignments.best_quote: She was like a woman of Leonardo da Vinci's, whom we love not so much for herself as for the things that she will not tell us

assignments.text:
That evening and all that night the water ran away. On the morrow the pool had
shrunk to its old size and lost its glory. It had been a call to the blood and
to the relaxed will, a passing benediction whose influence did not pass, a
holiness, a spell, a momentary chalice for youth.
assignments.summary: The pond returns to its ordinary size by the next day, but the moment it provided—a temporary Eden, a call to natural freedom—retains its spiritual significance even as its physical manifestation vanishes.
assignments.best_quote: It had been a call to the blood and to the relaxed will, a passing benediction whose influence did not pass, a holiness, a spell, a momentary chalice for youth.

assignments.text:
It did not do to think, nor, for the matter of that, to feel. She gave up
trying to understand herself, and joined the vast armies of the benighted, who
follow neither the heart nor the brain, and march to their destiny by
catch-words. The armies are full of pleasant and pious folk. But they have
yielded to the only enemy that matters—the enemy within. They have sinned
against passion and truth, and vain will be their strife after virtue. As the
years pass, they are censured. Their pleasantry and their piety show cracks,
their wit becomes cynicism, their unselfishness hypocrisy; they feel and
produce discomfort wherever they go. They have sinned against Eros and against
Pallas Athene, and not by any heavenly intervention, but by the ordinary course
of nature, those allied deities will be avenged.
assignments.summary: The narrator warns that those who surrender to self-deception and conformity, who follow catch-words instead of heart or brain, commit a sin against passion and truth; their virtue becomes hypocrisy, their wit cynicism.
assignments.best_quote: They have sinned against Eros and against Pallas Athene, and not by any heavenly intervention, but by the ordinary course of nature, those allied deities will be avenged

template.name: Thematic Currents: Propriety, Freedom, and Becoming
preferred_arcs: George Emerson's philosophy of being yourself

assignments.arc_name: George Emerson's philosophy of being yourself
assignments.text:
For a moment the original trouble was in the background. George would seem to
have behaved like a cad throughout; perhaps that was the view which one would
take eventually. At present she neither acquitted nor condemned him; she did
not pass judgement. At the moment when she was about to judge him her cousin’s
voice had intervened, and, ever since, it was Miss Bartlett who had dominated;
Miss Bartlett who, even now, could be heard sighing into a crack in the
partition wall; Miss Bartlett, who had really been neither pliable nor humble
nor inconsistent. She had worked like a great artist; for a time—indeed,
for years—she had been meaningless, but at the end there was presented to
the girl the complete picture of a cheerless, loveless world in which the young
rush to destruction until they learn better—a shamefaced world of
precautions and barriers which may avert evil, but which do not seem to bring
good, if we may judge from those who have used them most.
assignments.summary: Forster's narrative voice assesses Charlotte's manipulation as artistic: she has systematically painted for Lucy a bleak vision of a world of precaution and barriers that may prevent evil but do not bring good.
assignments.best_quote: She had worked like a great artist; for a time—indeed, for years—she had been meaningless, but at the end there was presented to the girl the complete picture of a cheerless, loveless world in which the young rush to destruction until they learn better

assignments.arc_name: George Emerson's philosophy of being yourself
assignments.text:
“Apparently. I told him it was unwise.” He would look no one in the face;
perhaps defeat was particularly mortifying for him. He alone had played
skilfully, using the whole of his instinct, while the others had used scraps of
their intelligence. He alone had divined what things were, and what he wished
them to be. He alone had interpreted the message that Lucy had received five
days before from the lips of a dying man. Persephone, who spends half her life
in the grave—she could interpret it also. Not so these English. They gain
knowledge slowly, and perhaps too late.
assignments.summary: The driver reveals his superiority of understanding: only he and Persephone grasp the significance of Lucy's encounter, while the English gain knowledge slowly and too late.
assignments.best_quote: He alone had interpreted the message that Lucy had received five days before from the lips of a dying man.

assignments.arc_name: George Emerson's philosophy of being yourself
assignments.text:
“Well, I am no prude. There is no need to call him a wicked young man, but
obviously he is thoroughly unrefined. Let us put it down to his deplorable
antecedents and education, if you wish. But we are no farther on with our
question. What do you propose to do?”
assignments.summary: Charlotte claims not to be prudish while systematically condemning George's class background and moral character, attributing his behavior to inferior upbringing.
assignments.best_quote: Well, I am no prude. There is no need to call him a wicked young man, but obviously he is thoroughly unrefined.

assignments.arc_name: George Emerson's philosophy of being yourself
assignments.text:
Lucy obeyed. She was in her cousin’s power. She could not modulate out the key
of self-abasement in which she had started. Neither of them referred again to
her suggestion that she should speak to George and settle the matter, whatever
it was, with him.
assignments.summary: Lucy is now fully in Charlotte's power; unable to assert her own will, she remains trapped in self-abasement. Neither of them mention her earlier suggestion to speak directly with George.
assignments.best_quote: She could not modulate out the key of self-abasement in which she had started.

assignments.text: “No, you don’t,” she snapped. “You don’t know what the word means.”
assignments.summary: Lucy sharply denies Cecil's claim to believe in democracy and accuses him of not understanding the word.
assignments.best_quote: No, you don't. You don't know what the word means.

template.name: Closing: The View with a Room – What Lucy Chooses

assignments.text:
“It isn’t fair, Cecil. I blame you—I blame you very much indeed. You had
no business to undo my work about the Miss Alans, and make me look ridiculous.
You call it scoring off Sir Harry, but do you realize that it is all at my
expense? I consider it most disloyal of you.”
assignments.summary: Lucy denounces Cecil for manipulating the villa situation at her expense and for betraying her trust.
assignments.best_quote: You had no business to undo my work about the Miss Alans, and make me look ridiculous. You call it scoring off Sir Harry, but do you realize that it is all at my expense? I consider it most disloyal of you.

assignments.text:
Secrecy has this disadvantage: we lose the sense of proportion; we cannot tell
whether our secret is important or not. Were Lucy and her cousin closeted with
a great thing which would destroy Cecil’s life if he discovered it, or with a
little thing which he would laugh at? Miss Bartlett suggested the former.
Perhaps she was right. It had become a great thing now. Left to herself, Lucy
would have told her mother and her lover ingenuously, and it would have
remained a little thing. “Emerson, not Harris”; it was only that a few weeks
ago. She tried to tell Cecil even now when they were laughing about some
beautiful lady who had smitten his heart at school. But her body behaved so
ridiculously that she stopped.
assignments.summary: Forster reflects that Lucy's inability to confess George's past to Cecil has transformed a minor incident into a grave secret, paralyzing her with shame whenever she attempts revelation.
assignments.best_quote: Secrecy has this disadvantage: we lose the sense of proportion; we cannot tell whether our secret is important or not.

assignments.text:
It is obvious enough for the reader to conclude, “She loves young Emerson.” A
reader in Lucy’s place would not find it obvious. Life is easy to chronicle,
but bewildering to practice, and we welcome “nerves” or any other shibboleth
that will cloak our personal desire. She loved Cecil; George made her nervous;
will the reader explain to her that the phrases should have been reversed?
assignments.summary: The narrator directly addresses the reader, noting that what is obvious to us (Lucy loves George) is invisible to Lucy herself, who takes refuge in social language to hide her true feelings.
assignments.best_quote: Life is easy to chronicle, but bewildering to practice, and we welcome "nerves" or any other shibboleth that will cloak our personal desire.
